::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## The decision this serves
What concentration must we achieve, and for how long? Every dose recommendation
ultimately traces back to a target occupancy someone decided was necessary — and
this lesson is the arithmetic that connects the two.
:::

## 1. The law of mass action

`P-02` established that binding is reversible. Write it down:

$$D + R \underset{k_{off}}{\overset{k_{on}}{\rightleftharpoons}} DR$$

Drug $D$ meets receptor $R$ at a rate proportional to how much of each is
present; the complex $DR$ falls apart at a rate proportional to how much complex
exists.

$$\frac{d[DR]}{dt} = k_{on}[D][R] - k_{off}[DR]$$

At equilibrium the two rates balance, and rearranging gives the **dissociation
constant**:

$$K_d = \frac{k_{off}}{k_{on}} = \frac{[D][R]}{[DR]}$$

$K_d$ has units of concentration, and a small $K_d$ means tight binding. It
carries a useful physical meaning: **$K_d$ is the free drug concentration at
which half the targets are occupied.**

## 2. The occupancy curve

Let $f$ be the fraction of targets occupied. Assuming drug is in vast excess over
target — usually true, and revisited below — the algebra gives:

$$f = \frac{[D]}{[D] + K_d}$$

This is the Langmuir isotherm, and it is the single most important curve in
pharmacology. Its shape has consequences that catch people out:

| Free concentration | Occupancy |
|---|---|
| 0.1 × K~d~ | 9% |
| **1 × K~d~** | **50%** |
| 9 × K~d~ | 90% |
| 99 × K~d~ | 99% |

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
Read that table again. Going from half occupancy to 90% costs a **ninefold**
increase in concentration. Getting to 99% costs **ninety-nine fold**.

This is why "just increase the dose until the target is fully blocked" is so
often impossible: the concentration required has climbed into the range where
selectivity is lost and off-targets are engaged. The therapeutic window is,
in large part, this curve running into that one.
:::

Plotted against log concentration, the curve becomes the familiar sigmoid, and
it spans about two log units from 10% to 90% occupancy. That number — **an
81-fold concentration range covers 10% to 90% effect** — is worth carrying
around. When a real dose–response looks steeper than that, something other than
simple binding is happening: cooperativity, a cascade, or a threshold. `P-14`
picks that up as the Hill coefficient.

## 3. Rates, not just ratios

$K_d$ is a ratio, so the same affinity can be built from very different rates.
Two drugs with $K_d$ = 1 nM:

- Drug A: $k_{on}$ fast, $k_{off}$ fast — binds quickly, leaves quickly
- Drug B: $k_{on}$ slow, $k_{off}$ slow — takes a while to engage, then stays

**Residence time** is $1/k_{off}$: the average time a molecule stays bound. Drug
B has a long one, and its effect can persist well after plasma concentrations
have fallen — the drug is gone from blood and still occupying its target.

This decouples effect from concentration, and it is a real strategy: several
modern drugs are optimised for slow dissociation rather than for affinity.
For a modeller it means a PK/PD model driven by plasma concentration will
mispredict unless the binding kinetics enter the model explicitly.

The notebook computes, for a realistic $K_d$ of 120 nM and $k_{on}$ of
10⁵ M⁻¹s⁻¹: a residence time of **83 seconds** and a dissociation half-life of
**58 seconds**. Fast — this is a conventional, rapidly reversible drug, and for
it the equilibrium assumption is safe.

### How long until equilibrium?

Approach to equilibrium is exponential with rate $k_{on}[D] + k_{off}$, so
reaching 90% of equilibrium occupancy takes about $2.3 / (k_{on}[D] + k_{off})$.

Counterintuitively, **higher concentrations equilibrate faster**. At
1 × K~d~ the notebook gets 96 seconds; at 10 × K~d~, 17 seconds. Either way it is
seconds to minutes, against plasma concentrations that change over hours — which
is what licenses treating binding as instantaneous in most PK/PD models. State
that assumption rather than inheriting it, and check it whenever a drug is
engineered for slow off-rates.

## 4. What an IC₅₀ actually measures

You will be handed IC₅₀ values constantly. An IC₅₀ is the concentration that
halves a *measured signal in a particular assay* — which means it depends on the
assay, not only on the drug.

In a competition experiment the drug must displace something else, so the more
competitor present, the more drug is needed and the weaker the drug appears.
The **Cheng–Prusoff** relationship converts back:

$$K_i = \frac{IC_{50}}{1 + [L]/K_{d,L}}$$

The notebook works an example: an IC₅₀ of 250 nM corresponds to a $K_i$ of
227 nM when the competing ligand is at 0.1 × its own K~d~, but only **23 nM**
when it is at 10 ×. Same drug, same target, a tenfold spread in apparent potency
— determined entirely by what else was in the well.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**An IC₅₀ without its assay conditions is not usable.** Before carrying one into
a model, ask what the competitor was and at what concentration. $K_i$ and $K_d$
are properties of the drug–target pair; IC₅₀ is a property of an experiment.
:::

## 5. Connecting to a real compound

`CASE-SM`'s Ozanib has a free peak of 96 nM and a free trough of 8.9 nM
(`S0-02` derived those from total concentrations and $f_u$ = 0.08). Against a
target with $K_d$ = 120 nM, the notebook computes:

- **peak occupancy 45%**
- **trough occupancy 7%**

So this regimen never approaches saturation and occupancy swings wildly across
the dosing interval. Whether that is a problem is a pharmacology question — some
targets need sustained blockade, others respond to intermittent high occupancy —
but you cannot even ask it without this calculation. It takes one line, and it is
routinely skipped.

### Occupancy can be measured, not only inferred

Everything above computes occupancy from a plasma concentration and a $K_d$
determined *in vitro*. That is an inference with two assumptions inside it:
that free concentration at the target equals free concentration in plasma, and
that the *in vitro* $K_d$ transfers to tissue. Both are testable.

Molecular imaging tests them directly. In a PET or SPECT competition study a
trace amount of a labelled ligand binds the target, unlabelled drug displaces it,
and the resulting signal gives **fractional occupancy in the tissue itself** as a
function of measured plasma concentration (Burvenich et al., AAPS J 2018,
[DOI](https://doi.org/10.1208/s12248-018-0203-z)). The output is an occupancy–
concentration curve obtained in the patient rather than in a well, which is what
lets a dose-selection argument say "this dose saturates the target" and mean it
literally.

Two things follow for a modeller. First, when such data exist they belong in the
model as observations, not as a validation afterthought. Second, when they do
not exist, the occupancy numbers above remain a calculation resting on stated
assumptions — worth writing down as assumptions, in the model report, where
`S0-06` will look for them.

## Work through it

- [Notebook — R](notebook-r.qmd)
- [Notebook — Python](notebook-py.qmd)

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```r
occupancy <- function(conc, Kd) conc / (conc + Kd)

Kd <- 120e-9                       # M
occupancy(c(0.1, 1, 9, 99) * Kd, Kd)     # 9%, 50%, 90%, 99%

kon  <- 1e5                        # 1/(M*s)
koff <- kon * Kd
c(residence_time_s = 1 / koff, dissociation_half_life_s = log(2) / koff)
```

### Python

```python
def occupancy(conc, Kd):
    return conc / (conc + Kd)

Kd = 120e-9                        # M
[occupancy(m * Kd, Kd) for m in (0.1, 1, 9, 99)]   # 9%, 50%, 90%, 99%

kon = 1e5                          # 1/(M*s)
koff = kon * Kd
1 / koff, np.log(2) / koff         # residence time, dissociation half-life
```

:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Failure mode — assuming drug is in excess when it is not
The occupancy formula above assumes free drug concentration is unchanged by
binding — fine when drug molecules vastly outnumber targets.

For a monoclonal antibody against a circulating target, that assumption
collapses. Target concentrations can be comparable to drug concentrations, so
binding **consumes** a meaningful fraction of the drug. Free drug is then no
longer what you dosed, occupancy is lower than the simple formula predicts, and
the bound complex is itself cleared — so the target is *eliminating the drug*.

The correct treatment is the quadratic binding equation, and beyond that the
target-mediated disposition models of `S1`. The failure is not using the simple
formula; it is using it without checking whether target concentration is
negligible. The notebook makes you check.
:::

### What comes after the quadratic

Once binding consumes drug, binding becomes *pharmacokinetics* — the bound
complex is cleared, so the target eliminates the drug. The standard treatment
(Dua, Hawkins & van der Graaf, [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.41), free full
text) sets out a ladder of models, and the useful part is the conditions under
which each simplification is allowed:

| Model | Assumes | Reliable for | Not reliable for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Full TMDD** | nothing beyond mass action | everything | needs data you rarely have |
| **Quasi-equilibrium (QE)** | binding and dissociation equilibrate fast | the linear terminal phase; clearance at high dose | the initial rapid fall in free target; short studies |
| **Quasi-steady-state (QSS)** | binding balanced by dissociation *plus* internalisation | the long phase where free target ≈ 0 | the initial fast phase and the terminal phase |
| **Michaelis–Menten (MM)** | target essentially saturated | high doses; sparse or incomplete data | low doses, where the target is not saturated |

Two things follow. **QE and QSS are not interchangeable**: if you need a terminal
half-life, QE is the one that gives it, and QSS is the one that does not. And
the ladder is chosen by which *phase of the curve* your question lives in — not
by which model converges.

This is exactly the kind of judgement that cannot be reconstructed from first
principles in an afternoon, which is why `S1` teaches it against a published
tutorial rather than from scratch.

## Check yourself

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Why does going from 90% to 99% occupancy cost eleven times more drug than reaching 90% did?
Because occupancy saturates. From $f = [D]/([D]+K_d)$, 90% needs 9 × K~d~ and 99%
needs 99 × K~d~ — an extra 90 × K~d~ on top of the 9 × K~d~ you already had. Each
additional increment of occupancy costs disproportionately more drug, and the
extra concentration is being spent in the range where off-target binding grows.
This is why programmes targeting near-complete inhibition are so much harder than
those needing partial blockade, and why the required occupancy should be argued
for explicitly rather than assumed to be "as much as possible".
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. A drug has K~d~ = 1 nM and a dissociation half-life of 6 hours. What does the second number change?
It decouples effect from plasma concentration. With a 6-hour dissociation
half-life, targets bound at C~max~ are still substantially occupied many hours
later, even as plasma concentration falls. Effect will lag and outlast exposure,
a concentration–effect plot will show hysteresis, and a direct-effect model will
fit badly or produce a meaningless EC₅₀. It also opens a dosing option: a
regimen that produces brief high peaks may sustain occupancy perfectly well,
which a concentration-driven model would never suggest.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Your *in vitro* colleagues report IC₅₀ = 50 nM. What do you ask before using it?
What the assay measured and what was competing. Specifically: was it a binding
assay or a functional one; what was the competing ligand or substrate and at what
concentration relative to its own K~d~ or K~m~ (for Cheng–Prusoff); was there
protein in the medium, since serum albumin binds drug and raises apparent IC₅₀;
and is 50 nM total or free. Any of these can move the number several-fold — which
is the difference between a dose that works and one that does not.
:::

  disposition* ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.41), free full text) picks up
  exactly where §5 of this lesson stops.

*Seen in the wild:* a candidate was selected on a tenfold affinity advantage over
its competitor. In patients the two were indistinguishable — both saturated the
target at clinical doses, and the extra affinity bought nothing. The occupancy
calculation that would have shown this takes a minute and was never done.
